card.hook: Fenway is squeezed into a packed city block, so forget stepping back for a big sweeping shot. The fun here is close-up and street-level, and your phone is great at that.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jersey Street, across from the main gate at 4 Jersey Street. Face east, with the ballpark in front of you and the Red Sox logo gate right ahead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the gate and the street together. If the pavement is crowded and you can't step back, try zoom 0.5x. For a tighter shot of the Red Sox logo, go to zoom 2x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the gate centred and hold your phone level so the gate and building edges stay straight.
card.best_time: Daytime outside game hours is likely to give you the clearest view of the gate. Before games the street can get busy, so give yourself extra time and patience, and take a few shots in case people walk through.
card.selfie_here: Try the Ted Williams statue on Jersey Street, or the Red Sox Teammates statue at the corner of Ipswich Street and Van Ness Street, near Gate B. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold the statue over your shoulder, but check your screen first, as we can't promise the ballpark will be behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Fenway is private property, so photo shoots inside the stadium generally need to be arranged in advance with the Red Sox events team. Going inside the park needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the gate dead centre with a banner on each side and not a single stranger walking through. Good luck!
card.good_to_know: Fenway is the home of the Boston Red Sox and the oldest active ballpark in Major League Baseball. The first game was played on 20 April 1912. The Green Monster, the tall left-field wall, took its present form at 37 feet high in the 1934 rebuild, and it's still painted in dark Dartmouth Green.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jersey Street, across from the main gate at 4 Jersey Street. Face east, with the ballpark in front of you and the Red Sox logo gate right ahead.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: the most famous wooden warship in America looks tiny from Piers Park. That's the charm, because you get the whole harbour with her small, recognisable shape sitting in it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piers Park on the East Boston waterfront and face north-west across the harbour. The ship is about 1.9 km away.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the wide harbour scene, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring her a bit closer. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the shoreline on a lower line and the ship on a grid crossing instead of dead centre, then tap the ship and slide the picture a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: The light depends on the time of day and the weather. Try to have the sun behind or beside you, not in front of you.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the ship behind you, head to the outdoor patio of the USS Constitution Museum at the Charlestown Navy Yard, facing the ship. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck her in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you with the ship in the distance, try asking a passer-by on Commercial Avenue in the North End, just left of the Coast Guard station where a concrete walkway runs out to the water (it's an older tip, so check it on the ground).
card.rules_and_safety: Piers Park is a free public park. The ship is reported to be closed on Mondays and major holidays, so check current hours before you go.
card.challenge: Take five frames at 2x-5x with your elbows on a rail, then pick the sharpest and see if a friend can spot the ship without you pointing.
card.good_to_know: USS Constitution, nicknamed Old Ironsides, is a three-masted wooden frigate launched in Boston in 1797. She's the oldest naval vessel still afloat, and she's still a commissioned US Navy ship with a crew of 75 officers and sailors. Her sailing cruises are rare, so don't plan around seeing her under sail.

card.hook: Look up over the Back Bay rooftops and there it is: a tall, plain glass tower that locals just call the Pru. It's so straight and simple that it makes the whole skyline look tidy.
card.stand_here: Stand in Copley Square on the Boylston Street side. The tower is about 580 m (a short walk) to the south-west of the square. Face south-west and it rises above the rooftops.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the tower and the Copley Square buildings in one frame. Try zoom 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground, and zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the top floors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line one up with the tower's edge, so it stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you the clearest view of the whole tower. On an evening when a big game is on, the windows sometimes light up to spell messages, so stay after dark and switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, step back a little, and keep the phone upright. Switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, so the tower fits over your shoulder. At this distance the Pru will look small, so make sure it sits in the frame next to you.
card.rules_and_safety: Copley Square is public, but the tower is an office and shopping complex, so check the official site first if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Put a tree or building in one corner, line the tower up with a gridline, and see if you can get it perfectly straight in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The Prudential Tower has 52 floors and was completed in 1964. It's 749 feet (228 m) tall, or 907 feet (276 m) with its radio mast, which makes it Boston's second-tallest building after the John Hancock Tower. When it opened, it ended the Custom House Tower's long run as the tallest in the city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Copley Square on the Boylston Street side. The tower is about 580 m (a short walk) to the south-west of the square. Face south-west and it rises above the rooftops.

card.hook: Cows used to graze right where you're about to take your photo, and they never once looked up at the skyline. You will.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the top of Flagstaff Hill, by the Soldiers and Sailors Monument. Face southwest toward the Public Garden, and you'll see the Back Bay buildings rising above the tree line.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the trees and buildings fit together. If your phone has it, zoom 2x pulls the Back Bay skyline in closer. Zoom 0.5x is good for the monument or the open lawns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the buildings, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day and go before noon, when the light falls nicely on the buildings. If you're here in winter, Frog Pond turns into an ice rink, and that's when its skyline view looks best.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the small hill leading up to the Soldiers and Sailors Monument. Turn your back to the skyline and keep the Back Bay buildings over your shoulder. Try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, then check the screen to make sure the skyline lines up above the trees.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you with the pond, stand on the east side of Frog Pond facing west-southwest and have your passer-by stand between you and the water. It's a short stroll from the hill.
card.rules_and_safety: Boston Common is an open public park, but check the official site before you go in case of event closures.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the skyline on the upper line, and let branches fill both top corners like a leafy picture frame.
card.good_to_know: Boston Common is the oldest city park in the United States and covers about 50 acres. The town bought most of the land in the 1630s as shared ground, and cows were formally banned in 1830. It became a Boston Landmark in 1977.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the top of Flagstaff Hill, by the Soldiers and Sailors Monument. Face southwest toward the Public Garden, and you'll see the Back Bay buildings rising above the tree line.

card.hook: Picture a full-size tall ship with the Boston skyline stacked up behind it, and a bridge railing trying very hard to photobomb it. That's the Tea Party ships on Fort Point Channel, and with a little care you can beat the railing.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk of the Congress Street Bridge, just outside the museum entrance, and face the moored ships Eleanor and Beaver. The water, the ships and the city all fit in one frame from here.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the ships, the channel and the skyline together. Tap 2x to pick out the masts and rigging. Use 0.5x only if you want a big sky, and keep the ships away from the edges so they don't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the ships along the lower third, and tap the ships; if the sky is bright, slide it a little darker so the hulls and sails keep their detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon from the eastern sidewalk, when one guide says the light falls best on the ships. Early morning is a second option from Congress Street, with the sun rising behind them.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Samuel Adams statue on the museum's front plaza, which the museum itself recommends for photos. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and check on site what ends up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the eastern sidewalk of the Congress Street Bridge, just outside the museum entrance, while you stand with the ships and channel in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine outside the museum up to the point where you enter the ships. Photos and video aren't allowed inside the museum exhibit areas or with the costumed actors in the theatre, and sources differ on phones aboard the ships, so check the official site before you board.
card.challenge: Keep the masts perfectly upright and the bridge railing out of the shot, then wait for the people in the foreground to move away. Bonus points for a mock tea-tossing pose on deck, if you go aboard.
card.good_to_know: On the night of 16 December 1773, members of the Sons of Liberty, disguised as American Indians, boarded the merchant ship Dartmouth. They threw 340 or 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor. Today the story is told with the full-size replica ships Eleanor and Beaver.

card.hook: Picture a short cobbled lane tipping uphill between brick houses, with gas lamps along the way. It looks like a film set, and you barely have to try to get a good photo of it.
card.stand_here: Head to Acorn Street at the West Cedar Street end, at the bottom of the block, where the phone icon on the map marks the street. Face up the lane towards Willow Street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which shows the lane about the way your eye sees it. Use 0.5x only if you're very close, because it can stretch the buildings at the edges. Try 2x for a tighter shot of the lamps and cobbles climbing the hill.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the middle of the lane on the centre line and keep your phone level so the brick fronts don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds arrive. Late afternoon is also a good time.
card.selfie_here: Try Acorn Street at its corner with Willow Street. Stand right at the intersection with the downhill slope of the lane behind you, so the cobbles and brick houses fill the frame. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the street stays over your shoulder. If you'd rather stay out of the lane, pose on Mount Vernon Street just before its junction with Willow Street, facing up or down the hill.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the bottom of the lane, at the West Cedar Street end, and frame you with the whole street climbing up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here and Acorn Street is a private way, so keep to the roadway, don't block doorways and don't point your phone into open windows. Stay off private stoops, steps and front gardens. Casual phone photos don't need a permit, but professional shoots do, through the Acorn Street Association. The cobbles are uneven and can be slippery when wet or icy, so wear flat shoes and watch your footing while you look at the screen.
card.challenge: Can you get one shot of the lane with nobody in the roadway? Be patient, because the gap always comes if you wait a moment.
card.good_to_know: Acorn Street is a one-block lane between West Cedar Street and Willow Street. It's lined with Federal-style brick houses, gas lamps and cobblestones. The straight view up the lane between the brick fronts is the one most visitors photograph.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Acorn Street at the West Cedar Street end, at the bottom of the block, where the phone icon on the map marks the street. Face up the lane towards Willow Street.

card.hook: There's a golden grasshopper perched on top of this red-brick hall, and most people walk right under it without looking up. Faneuil Hall rewards the people who do.
card.stand_here: Stand in Dock Square, on the western side of the hall, and face the building so the whole front fills your frame across the open space. Let a few people walk through the bottom of the shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the full facade. Switch to 0.5x if you're close or the square is packed. Then zoom in as far as your phone allows (2x or higher) to pick out the little cupola and its grasshopper weathervane.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter, and summer afternoons can get very busy. One guide says the hall looks great with Quincy Market around blue hour, when the dome is lit. If you try that, turn on night mode and rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Head to the bronze Samuel Adams statue on the granite plaza in front of the hall, on the Congress Street side. Use the front camera, stand beside the statue, and keep Faneuil Hall behind your shoulder. Try 0.5x if you want more of the building in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Dock Square facing the Samuel Adams statue, while you stand by the statue so they can fit you and the hall together.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the open public squares around it. If you want to go inside, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the grasshopper weathervane sharp and clear in your shot, with no heads in the way?
card.good_to_know: Faneuil Hall opened in 1742 and was designed by the artist John Smibert. It's nicknamed "the Cradle of Liberty" because of the speeches and debates held inside. Charles Bulfinch enlarged it in 1806, so you're seeing a mix of old and newer. It's also a stop on the Freedom Trail.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Dock Square, on the western side of the hall, and face the building so the whole front fills your frame across the open space. Let a few people walk through the bottom of the shot.

card.hook: Copley Square is a handy history lesson: a grand Beaux-Arts library, Trinity Church and the glass Hancock Tower all squeezed into one view. The library is one of the easiest big buildings in Boston to photograph, because the square gives you room to back up.
card.stand_here: Stand in Copley Square, across Boylston Street from the library's main McKim façade. Face the library so the whole width of the building fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the library, Trinity Church and the Hancock Tower together. Switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of the library front alone, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the arched doors and the sculpture on the steps.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so the building stands straight, and if the sky looks washed out, tap the library front and slide it a bit darker.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is best, when the library front is in shade and the light is softer. The square sometimes hosts events and a farmers market in season, so give yourself time to move along and find a clear gap.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the library steps on Boylston Street, using the shaded side of the façade so the building fills the frame behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the arches stay over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Copley Square, across the street from the library, while you pose on the library steps, so the whole McKim façade and the square fit in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photos for personal use are generally fine inside the library, but skip the flash and be respectful of other visitors. One photographer reports that posed photography isn't allowed during business hours, and professional shoots may need permits, so check the library's official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Fit the library, Trinity Church and the Hancock Tower into one 0.5x shot without cutting off a single roofline.
card.good_to_know: The library was authorised by a Massachusetts statute in 1848 and officially established by a city ordinance in 1852. Its Reading Room opened in 1854 in a former schoolhouse on Mason Street. The Copley Square building became a Boston Landmark in 2000, and with around 24 million items the library is the third-largest public library in the United States.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Copley Square, across Boylston Street from the library's main McKim façade. Face the library so the whole width of the building fits in your frame.

card.hook: This church has no steeple, and that's the story. The builders ran out of money, so you get a sturdy granite block of a building instead, which looks great in photos.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Tremont Street and School Street, at the front of the chapel, and face the entrance. Step back far enough to keep the columns straight, and keep passers-by on the pavement out of the bottom of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole front. If traffic or the pavement stops you stepping back, try 0.5x, but keep the chapel away from the edges so the lines don't lean. Use 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the column tops, the stonework, or Park Street Church's steeple down the street.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines, then tap the stone front and make the picture a little darker if the sky is bright so the granite keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or a bright overcast day, is worth trying for bringing out the texture of the stone. If people wander through your shot, take a few frames and keep the cleanest one.
card.selfie_here: Try King's Chapel Burying Ground, next to the chapel at 58 Tremont Street, where the weathered gravestones make a moody backdrop. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low. Have a look over your shoulder first, because we couldn't confirm the chapel will be right behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Tremont Street, facing the chapel's stone front, while you stand at the Tremont and School Street corner in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: In the burying ground, keep to the paths. Rules for going inside the chapel can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the columns, the granite and Park Street Church's steeple all fit in one frame, then take it without a single stranger in the bottom edge.
card.good_to_know: The King's Chapel congregation began in 1686 as the first Anglican church in colonial New England. The stone building, designed by Peter Harrison, went up between 1749 and 1754 around the old wooden church, which was then carried out through the new windows. Plans for a steeple were dropped when money ran short.

card.hook: Down at street level, Quincy Market is a happy scrum of performers, snack queues and strollers, and you can't tell it's actually three buildings in a row. Go up for the view that makes it all click.
card.stand_here: Stand on the observation deck at Custom House Tower and look down at the market. You'll see the three Quincy Market roofs below you, with Faneuil Hall alongside and the skyline behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the whole view from the deck. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in more skyline, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the three roofs and Faneuil Hall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the three roofs up with a grid line so they sit straight, then keep a little skyline in the top third.
card.best_time: One guide suggests blue hour, just after sunset when the city lights come on. Switch on night mode if your phone has it.
card.selfie_here: Head inside the central building and stand under the Great Dome in the rotunda. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the dome fill the space over your shoulder. For a granite backdrop, sit on the front steps of the central building facing the pedestrian walkway, and go early in the day to dodge photobombers.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, the food hall is lively but crowded, so be considerate of stallholders and other visitors when you take photos. The Custom House deck is described as open to the public, but check the official site for admission and opening times before you go.
card.challenge: Count the three market roofs, then find Faneuil Hall tucked in beside them, and get all four into one straight-lined shot.
card.good_to_know: Quincy Market was finished in 1826 and designed by Alexander Parris. It's the central one of three buildings, with a domed middle section and a porticoed end on each side. Since 1976 the whole group has been the Faneuil Hall Marketplace, and it's a stop on the Freedom Trail.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the observation deck at Custom House Tower and look down at the market. You'll see the three Quincy Market roofs below you, with Faneuil Hall alongside and the skyline behind.

card.hook: Everything around North Square is brick, and then there's this little wooden house with its top floor poking out over the street like it's leaning in to gossip. It looks so different from its neighbours that it's hard to walk past.
card.stand_here: Stand in North Square, across the square from the front of the house on the 19 North Square side. Face south-west towards 19 North Square and you'll get the whole gabled front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full front of the house. If the square feels too cramped to fit it all in, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for the overhang, windows and gable.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the house up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softest. Morning is lovely here because the sun hits the old wooden front.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the cobbles in North Square with the house's wooden front right behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tilt it up a little so the overhang and gable show over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Rachel Revere Park, across the street from the house, while you stand on the cobbles in North Square with the house behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules inside the museum may differ from outside, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Find the brick courtyard beside the house and get a shot of the bronze bell cast by Revere (if you can see it), then try to fit the overhang, gable and windows into one picture.
card.good_to_know: The house was built no later than 1680, and Paul Revere owned it between 1770 and 1800. It opened as a museum in 1908 after a renovation. It's also the only house on the Freedom Trail, sitting between Faneuil Hall and Old North Church.

card.hook: A rough concrete block, a glass wing bolted on the side, and seals splashing out front: this is one of Boston's more unusual waterfront scenes. You don't even need a ticket to get a good photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Central Wharf plaza, in front of the aquarium entrance. From here the aquarium's main facade is just to the north-east, with the harbour and moored boats beside it, so face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole facade and the harbour in one frame, then try 1x for a more natural view. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the seals or for close details of the concrete and glass.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the concrete and water. Midday can be glary on the glass and harbour, so check the weather first.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the Central Wharf plaza with the aquarium building behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and tilt it slightly up so the building lands over your shoulder.

card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are on the aquarium's prohibited items list, so leave yours at home. Flash is not allowed near sensitive exhibits. Stay back from the water's edge while you compose.
card.challenge: Collect a set of three: the whole building, a close-up of a seal (tap on the animal and take a quick burst), and the whale mural next door.
card.good_to_know: The concrete main building opened in 1969 and was designed by Peter Chermayeff of Cambridge Seven Associates. The glass-and-steel West Wing was added in 1998. The harbor seal exhibit at the front can be watched for free, at any hour, without going inside.

card.hook: Picture a little brick building holding its ground between glass towers, like it showed up first and refuses to move. It did: the Old State House dates from 1713, and the skyscrapers are the newcomers.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of State Street and Congress Street, with the Old State House to the west of you. Face it and you get the classic Freedom Trail postcard view, old brick in front of the newer buildings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the postcard shot. If the building and the towers behind it won't both fit, tap 0.5x. For the lion and unicorn and the tower on top, zoom 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower on the centre line so the building stands up straight, and leave a little sky above it.
card.best_time: Dusk is the winner, when the windows glow against the sky. Court Street gives a diagonal view just as the lights come on.
card.selfie_here: Go to the foot of State Street and turn your back on the building. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and tap 0.5x so the brick front fits behind your shoulder. Early morning is quietest, so you'll have the street almost to yourself.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner of State Street and Congress Street, then pose with the building behind you so it's the postcard shot with you in it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside from the public pavement are fine. The museum inside has limited photography, so check the official site before you go. Keep an eye on the busy pavement while you line up your shot.
card.challenge: Get the brick front and a glass skyscraper in one frame with the tower dead centre, then spot the lion and unicorn up on the gable.
card.good_to_know: The Old State House is Boston's oldest surviving public building. In the 18th century it housed the colonial and state governments, and today it's a history museum. At 65 feet (20 metres) it was the tallest building in Boston until 1745.

card.hook: Most photo spots make you fight the crowd, the clutter and the wires. Here it's just one tall, pale granite shape standing on a green lawn, and almost nothing competes with it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lawn side of Monument Square, in the park around the monument, and face north-west, because that's where the obelisk is. Hold your phone upright so the whole height fits.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, held upright, which should fit the whole obelisk with some sky above it. Walk closer to the base or want the lawn and trees in too? Switch to 0.5x and keep the phone level. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the pointed top and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the shaft up with a vertical line, because an obelisk that leans looks wrong; tap the stone, and if the sky is washing out, slide it a touch darker so the granite keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a quieter lawn. The monument's exterior is lit at night, so an evening shot works too: use night mode and tuck your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze statue of Colonel William Prescott near the base of the obelisk, use the front camera, and let the monument rise behind you (try 0.5x if your phone offers it). The grassy hill around the obelisk is another good backdrop, with trees down both sides of the frame. Check what's behind you before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Massachusetts gate and shoot back toward the obelisk while you pose on the lawn in front of it, so the whole monument fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: The monument has steep, narrow stairs where people can't pass each other easily, and space at the top is limited. The interior and top may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the obelisk dead straight against a gridline, with a tree in each lower corner like curtains on a stage.
card.good_to_know: The Battle of Bunker Hill was fought here on Breed's Hill on 17 June 1775. The monument was designed by Solomon Willard, built between 1825 and 1843, and dedicated on 17 June 1843. At 221 feet (67 m), it was the largest obelisk in the United States when it was finished, and it's the last stop on the Freedom Trail after the USS Constitution.

card.hook: Look up from the Common and there it is: a gold dome sitting on top of a red-brick hill like it knows it's the star. It's hard to take a bad photo of it, and easy to take a great one.
card.stand_here: Stand in Boston Common, on the Beacon Street edge across from the State House, and face north up the hill. For a classic uphill view, wander down to the lower Common near the fountain.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole building, the dome and the lawns in one shot. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the dome and the little gilded pine cone on top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the gold keeps its glow against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Late afternoon light is lovely on the Beacon Street side in spring and autumn, and in autumn try to arrive before 5 PM. Morning light is also good for the dome.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps from the Common toward the building, then turn around with your front camera so the facade, columns and gold dome rise behind you. You can also try the front plaza just inside the low iron fence, facing the facade. A guide says it's largely clear early in the morning. Try 0.5x if your front camera has it, to squeeze in more of the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Common side of Beacon Street, far enough back to fit the full golden dome and white columns, while you pose on the steps up from the Common.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in the public areas, but check posted signs and ask security if you're unsure about a particular room. Interior photos are restricted in some areas, and tours may run on weekdays only, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a tree or a statue on the lawn and use it to frame the dome, like the State House is peeking out from behind it.
card.good_to_know: Charles Bulfinch designed the State House, and it was completed in January 1798. It's one of the oldest state capitols still in use. Paul Revere's company first covered the dome in copper in 1802, and it was re-gilded in 23k gold in 1997.

card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the steeple up with a vertical line so it stands straight, then let the street lead the eye down to the church.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun isn't directly behind the steeple. Arriving early in the day should mean a quieter street.
card.selfie_here: Head to Paul Revere Mall and stand next to the bronze Paul Revere statue, where the tip of the steeple peeks out above it. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the statue and steeple over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot and shuffle until the steeple tip shows.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Hull Street, about halfway up the hill, facing the church so the full front fits in the frame, while you step down the slope toward the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a working congregation, so go inside only if the doors are open, and check the official site first. Its visitor policy says photos are welcome except during worship services, but no flash (LED lights included) and no videos.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the steeple stands perfectly straight on a gridline and the street runs like a slide right down to the front door.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1723, and this is the oldest standing church in Boston. On the night of 18 April 1775, two lanterns were lit in the steeple to warn Patriots about British troop movements. The steeple is 191 feet (58 m) tall and dates from 1955, and the bell tower holds eight bells cast in 1744, the oldest in North America.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Hull Street, about halfway up the hill, and look down toward Salem Street. The brick front and white steeple of Old North Church sit right at the end of the sloping street, and you'll fit the whole front in one frame. Get much closer and it won't fit.

card.hook: Bronze ducklings in a neat line, willow trees behind them, and probably a few other people waiting for the same shot. It's a small spot, so a little patience pays off.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Charles Street and Beacon Street, near the bronze duckling statues (Make Way for Ducklings) on that side of the garden. Face the statues with the garden's trees and path behind them; the middle of the garden and the lagoon are to the south.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the ducklings. At the Lagoon Bridge, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the willow branches overhead, or try zoom 2x to cut out people and home in on the arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and crouch down so the line of ducklings sits level in the lower third, with the path and trees filling the background.
card.best_time: Go early, before the crowds build. The bridge gets very crowded from mid-morning. Tulips and magnolias peak from late April into early May, and the willows are lush from late spring through autumn.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto the Lagoon Bridge early in the morning and turn your back to the water and willows, with the front camera at zoom 0.5x so the scenery fits over your shoulder. Want fewer people? Try the lagoon bank on the west side near Arlington Street, which is less crowded than the paths and is good for sunrise light.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the lagoon bank facing the footbridge, so the whole bridge and its reflection in the water are behind you (the bridge is a busy walkway, so wait for a gap).
card.rules_and_safety: The City of Boston is said to require a permit for professional photo shoots, so check the official site if you're planning more than casual phone photos.
card.challenge: Get the whole line of ducklings in one picture with nobody else in the frame. Bonus points if you wait it out without sighing.
card.good_to_know: The Boston Public Garden was the first public botanical garden in America. It covers about 24 acres and was designed by George F. Meacham. The pond was finished in 1859, the wrought iron fence went up in 1862, and the suspension bridge over the pond dates from 1867.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Charles Street and Beacon Street, near the bronze duckling statues (Make Way for Ducklings) on that side of the garden. Face the statues with the garden's trees and path behind them; the middle of the garden and the lagoon are to the south.

card.hook: Look up at the Zakim Bridge and you'll see a giant harp, with cables fanned out like strings from two tall towers. The tops are shaped like obelisks, a nod to the Bunker Hill Monument just up the road.
card.stand_here: Stand at the eastern end of Paul Revere Park, where the towers rise above the lawn, and face south-west towards the bridge. The park has been getting reworked, so check the access before you head over.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the towers, the cables and the river in one shot. Try 0.5x to catch a whole tower and the sweep of the cables, then 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the obelisk tops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put a tower on one of the vertical lines, and let the cables fan out across the frame.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into evening usually suits the silhouette look. Around dusk you often get a softer sky behind the cables.
card.selfie_here: Stay at the eastern end of Paul Revere Park, where the towers rise above the lawn, and turn around so the bridge is behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x so more of the towers squeeze in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the park's big oval lawn while you stand toward the eastern end with the towers rising behind you (that's our best guess from the park's layout).
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is a live highway, so never stand on the roadway, the ramps or the shoulders. Keep to the park paths and lawn, and watch out for parking near the bridge, which can earn a ticket.
card.challenge: Get a silhouette so clean that the towers look like they were cut out of paper, then add a small you for scale.
card.good_to_know: The Zakim Bridge carries Interstate 93 over the Charles River at Charlestown. It was finished in 2003 as part of the Big Dig, and it replaced the 1950s Charlestown High Bridge. Guides often call this the classic Boston view of the bridge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the eastern end of Paul Revere Park, where the towers rise above the lawn, and face south-west towards the bridge. The park has been getting reworked, so check the access before you head over.

card.hook: Picture a huge stone church with a pool at its feet, doubling the towers whenever the water goes still. That's Trinity Church, and you don't need to be a photographer to get a good shot of it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Copley Square, in front of the church, facing its main facade. The church is to the east from here, so you'll see the stone towers with the reflecting pool in front and the Boston Public Library across the square.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and the pool in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the facade, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the tower, the arches and the stone detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the central tower up with the middle vertical line, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, when the sun sets over Old South Church and warms the stone. One photographer recommends August, and a calm moment on the pool gives you the best reflection.
card.selfie_here: Use the open plaza in front of Trinity Church in Copley Square: front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and the church over your shoulder. Fancy a bonus? The blue glass of the John Hancock Tower near Clarendon Street mirrors the church, so you can try a selfie there too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the front entrance of the Boston Public Library (700 Boylston St), facing the square, while you stand in front of Trinity Church.
card.rules_and_safety: The square and the outside of the church are open to the public. Inside opening hours vary, so check the official site first if you want to go in.
card.challenge: Crouch down by the pool's edge and see if you can get the water to fill the bottom third of your photo with the church repeated in it.
card.good_to_know: The congregation dates from 1733, but the church you see was built between 1872 and 1877, after the Great Boston Fire destroyed the earlier site on Summer Street. Henry Hobson Richardson designed it, and it's regarded as the birthplace of the Richardsonian Romanesque style, with rough Dedham Granite and heavy arches. The big central tower was designed by Stanford White, who was working in Richardson's office, and it was based on a tower in Salamanca, Spain.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Copley Square, in front of the church, facing its main facade. The church is to the east from here, so you'll see the stone towers with the reflecting pool in front and the Boston Public Library across the square.

card.hook: Right in the middle of busy Boston, a tall Egyptian-style gate stands guard over rows of crooked slate headstones. It's a ready-made picture frame, and it's free.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Tremont Street pavement at the cemetery's main entrance, at the corner of Tremont and Bromfield Street, directly opposite the Egyptian Revival arch. The middle of the cemetery is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west, so face the arch and the headstones behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole arch and the headstones beneath it. Only drop to 0.5x if people or traffic push you in close, and keep the arch in the middle so its sides don't lean. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for rows of headstones and carved details through the railings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the arch up with the centre line, then tap the headstones and drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out and the slate keeps its texture.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the carvings are clear, because low light makes this place hard to photograph. Tremont Street is busy with Freedom Trail walkers, so be patient and shoot between groups.
card.selfie_here: On the Tremont Street sidewalk, stand at the arched entrance with the burying ground behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the gate and gravestones sit over your shoulder. Inside, the tall obelisk on the path near the centre is a good second backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the public Tremont Street sidewalk facing the gate, while you stand at the arched entrance so the whole burying ground shows behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed, but be respectful of other visitors and the solemn nature of the site. It's described as free to visit, but opening times can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the arch dead centre on the grid with the Park Street Church spire peeking out above the trees, and no stranger's head in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Granary Burying Ground is Boston's third-oldest cemetery, founded in 1660. It has 2,345 grave-markers, and historians think as many as 5,000 people are buried here, including Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, John Hancock and the five Boston Massacre victims. The granite obelisk was put up in 1827 for Benjamin Franklin's parents and relatives.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Tremont Street pavement at the cemetery's main entrance, at the corner of Tremont and Bromfield Street, directly opposite the Egyptian Revival arch. The middle of the cemetery is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west, so face the arch and the headstones behind it.
